question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{7x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=7x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln4,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}\ln4\cdot 7 \\  & =7\ln4\cdot {4}^{u} \\  & =7\ln4\cdot {4}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{7}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/7} & =7\ln(4)\cdot {4}^{7(1/7)} \\  & =7\ln(4)\cdot 4 \\  & =28\ln(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}$ is $28\ln(4).$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=-1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=2x+1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}\ln(4),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}\ln(4)\cdot 2 \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\ln(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point. 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-1} & ={(2\cdot {4}^{2x+1}\ln4)|}_{x=-1} \\  & =2\cdot {4}^{-1}\ln(4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\ln(4) \\  & =\ln((4)^{1/2}) \\  & =\ln\,(\,\sqrt{4}) \\  & =\ln(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={({4}^{2x+1})|}_{x=-1} \\  & ={4}^{2(-1)+1} \\  & ={4}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\ln(2)\cdot (x+1) \\ y-\frac{1}{4} & =\ln(2)\,x+\ln(2) \\ y & =\ln(2)\,x+\ln(2)+\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
